title: Woke Enough to Be Left, Explicit Enough to Be Right
author: Kylie Hoey
summary: Victorian primary teacher Kylie Hoey asks why explicit instruction is so often tied to right-wing politics when she, a self-described left-of-centre teacher, advocates for it. Using humour and sarcasm, she points out that teachers accused of indoctrination would, if they really wanted students to absorb beliefs, do it through explicit instruction rather than inquiry. She then walks through the parts of the Victorian curriculum that critics call woke, including First Nations histories, sustainability and respectful relationships, and defends them as important and age-appropriate. Her central argument is that she came to explicit instruction out of anger at watching vulnerable Grade 6 students leave primary school unable to read and write, and she cites prison-entrant schooling statistics to show what is at stake. She sees explicit teaching as a form of social intervention and a social justice issue, notes that Victoria's Labor government mandated phonics, and concludes that the method itself is apolitical even if its advocates are a diverse group.
points: Hoey argues that explicit instruction is a means of educational equity, since knowledge and academic success level the playing field for the most disadvantaged students.

The claim that teachers indoctrinate students is undercut by the fact that explicit instruction, not inquiry, would be the most effective way to do so, which exposes the weakness of the political framing.
Her primary classroom practice on identity and diversity is about body safety and critical thinking about stereotypes, not pushing an agenda.
She cites that 29% of surveyed Australian prison entrants completed Year 9 or below, to show how poor schooling outcomes can compound.
Phonics and explicit teaching were mandated by Labor in Victoria and promoted across the aisle, suggesting the method belongs to no single political camp.
quotes: As an avid proponent of explicit instruction, I have been accused of boring students to death, ignoring curiosity and overlooking inclusion. But what I never expected to be called was fascist, far-right or authoritarian. But here we are.
For some strange reason, explicit instruction continues to be entangled with right-wing political ideologies and honestly, I find the whole thing rather perplexing.

This is actually hilarious because if I was going to spend my time indoctrinating students about any of these things, I’d absolutely do it through explicit instruction. Because, as it turns out, that’s how students learn best. I certainly wouldn’t be relying on an inquiry approach if my intention was to ensure students actually learnt what I wanted them to believe.

As a Grade 6 teacher, I watched far too many students graduate from primary school without being able to read and write proficiently. I was even angrier when those students came from socially or financially vulnerable families, knowing that the consequences of poor literacy were likely to be felt even more acutely by those who already had fewer opportunities and resources available to them.

I see explicit instruction as a form of social intervention. It is, fundamentally, a social justice issue. Knowledge and academic success help level the playing field. They provide students, particularly those from our most vulnerable communities, with opportunities, choices and pathways that they might otherwise never have access to.

Explicit instruction is a means of giving students the knowledge and skills they need to experience academic success. It is a protective factor in their educational trajectories, increasing their opportunities to access further education, employment and greater participation in society.

I place a strong emphasis on ensuring that the learning needs of my most at-risk students are not just acknowledged, but adequately catered for. And how do I do that? Through explicit instruction. Yes, I apparently use a right-wing weapon to gain educational equity.

I can safely say that explicit instruction itself is apolitical but the people that advocate for it are a unique, diverse bunch of individuals that are striving for the same thing. In a world that is increasingly divided into 2 politically aligned camps, it is a good thing that explicit instruction can at least bring us together. Let’s hope we can do the same with other topics that should never have been stereotyped politically in the first place.
